pathogen_scientific_name.quote: the causal agent of the mango dieback disease in the UAE is L. theobromae

type_of_disease.quote: different fungi associated with it ... Fungal pathogens, such as Neofusicoccum ribis, Botryosphaeria dothidea ... L. theobromae is a soil-borne wound pathogen

affected_parts.quote: The pathogen was observed to attack different parts of the mango trees. First, we noticed the disease symptoms in all plant tissues, including leaves, twigs, and apical tips ... discolouration of vascular regions of the stems and branches ... resulting in the eventual death of the whole tree

summary.value: Leaves roll upward and turn brown with a scorch-like appearance, then drop; twigs die back from tips inward toward vascular tissues. In advanced stages, branches dry out sequentially, vascular tissues brown, and the whole tree is defoliated and dies.
summary.quote: leaves, their margins roll upwards turning them a brownish colour. Later, a scorch-like appearance developed, followed by the dropping of the infected leaves. Moreover, twigs died from the tips back inwards (toward the vascular tissues), giving a scorched appearance to the branches ... branches dry out one after another in a sequence resulting in the eventual death of the whole tree

diagnostic_features.value: Twig tip dieback advancing inward with browning of vascular tissues visible on cross-section, combined with leaf margin rolling, browning, and scorch-like defoliation; symptoms progress sequentially branch by branch.
diagnostic_features.quote: twigs died from the tips back inwards (toward the vascular tissues) ... We observed browning in the vascular tissues when longitudinal cross-sections were made in diseased mango twigs ... twig tip dieback that advances into the old wood with branches that dry and die, and leaves scorch and fall

value: Mango dieback caused by Neofusicoccum ribis
Mango dieback caused by Botryosphaeria dothidea
Mango dieback caused by Diplodia sp.
Mango dieback caused by Pseudofusicoccum sp.
Mango dieback caused by Ceratocystis sp.
look_alikes.quote: Fungal pathogens, such as Neofusicoccum ribis, Botryosphaeria dothidea, Diplodia sp., Pseudofusicoccum sp., and Ceratocystis sp. may infect mango trees individually, or in combinations, to cause mango dieback in different parts of the world

type_of_disease.quote: There are many fungal species, mostly saprophytes (i.e., non-pathogens) that form sooty mould deposits on trees and shrubs

affected_parts.quote: large amounts of honeydew, and dense growths of sooty mould fungi over leaves and stems (Photos 1-4)

summary.value: Sooty moulds appear as dark, superficial fungal deposits on leaves and stems, growing on honeydew secreted by sap-sucking insects; the leaf remains green beneath the superficial mould layer. On mango, the fungal growth turns the leaf surface black.
summary.quote: The fungi that cause sooty moulds grow on the sugary substances that are produced by insects... The leaf is still green beneath the superficial mould.

diagnostic_features.value: Dark sooty deposits on the upper surface of leaves and stems; the leaf remains green beneath the superficial mould layer; does not infect plant tissue but blocks sunlight from reaching leaf chloroplasts; presence of sap-sucking insects (aphids, soft scale, leafhoppers, planthoppers, psyllids, whiteflies) is typically associated.
diagnostic_features.quote: The leaf is still green beneath the superficial mould. ... Often, their presence is a sign that sap-sucking insects are present... The fungi that cause sooty moulds grow on the sugary substances that are produced by insects - mostly, aphids, soft scale (not armoured scale), leafhoppers, planthoppers, psyllids and whiteflies

conflicts.note: The UF/IFAS source names Meliola mangiferae as the mango sooty mold species. The Lucid/PPPW source names Capnodium mangiferum specifically for mango. Multiple fungal species can cause sooty mould; both may be valid causal organisms.
UF/IFAS mentions only foliage; Lucid/PPPW records both leaves and stems.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Mango Gall Midge is a major pest of mango and is found in all mango growing countries of the world

affected_parts.quote: The larvae (maggots) bore inside leaf tissue, and feed within, resulting in formation of small raised wart-like galls on the leaves.

summary.value: Small raised wart-like galls form on leaves, resembling pimples, up to 3-4 mm in diameter. Heavily galled leaves curl up and drop prematurely, and small exit holes are visible where larvae leave the galls.
summary.quote: whose feeding induces the formation of small galls, which look like pimples on the leaves... resulting in formation of small raised wart-like galls on the leaves. Gall formation begins within seven days and attains a maximum diameter of about 3-4 mm. Heavily galled leaves curl up and drop off prematurely

diagnostic_features.value: Wart-like galls up to 3-4 mm diameter on leaves, with small emergence holes where larvae exit; heavily infested leaves curl and drop, causing dieback of whole branches in susceptible cultivars.
diagnostic_features.quote: Gall formation begins within seven days and attains a maximum diameter of about 3-4 mm... Small emergence holes may be detected where larvae leave the galls through, as they go to the soil for pupation... Heavily galled leaves curl up and drop off prematurely, causing dieback of whole branches in susceptible cultivars.

affected_parts.quote: Adult weevils feed on the surface of young leaves, causing them to turn brown, curl, and crumple. Plants infested by the weevils have visibly stripped shoots that can be seen from a distance.

summary.value: Adult weevils feed on the surface of young leaves, causing them to turn brown, curl, and crumple. Infested plants have visibly stripped shoots and pieces of young leaves found on the ground under the tree.
summary.quote: Adult weevils feed on the surface of young leaves, causing them to turn brown, curl, and crumple. Plants infested by the weevils have visibly stripped shoots that can be seen from a distance. Pieces of young leaves can often be found under the tree.

diagnostic_features.value: Stripped shoots visible from a distance on infested plants, combined with presence of leaf bits under the tree.
diagnostic_features.quote: Plants infested by the weevils have visibly stripped shoots that can be seen from a distance. Pieces of young leaves can often be found under the tree.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial black spot is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae (Gagnevin and Pruvost 2001, Ah-You et al. 2009).

type_of_disease.quote: Bacterial black spot is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae

affected_parts.quote: The causal agent of BBS (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae) infects stems, leaves, and fruit tissue through natural openings and wounds

summary.value: Leaf lesions appear as raised black angular spots with greasy margins following leaf venation, often surrounded by a chlorotic (yellow) halo. Fruit lesions begin as small irregular water-soaked specks or star-shaped lesions around lenticels that blacken, develop raised greasy margins, coalesce, and crack.
summary.quote: Leaf lesions appear as raised black angular spots, frequently developing greasy margins following leaf venation, and often surrounded by a chlorotic (yellow) halo. Symptoms on fruits begin as small irregular water-soaked specks around lenticels or as small star-shaped lesions. As the disease progresses, these lesions blacken, develop greasy margins that become raised and coalesce, and then develop cracks.

diagnostic_features.value: BBS lesions are angular and raised (not round and sunken), confined to the peel and upper pulp, darker, with raised margins that crack and ooze sap when coalescing. A tear-stain infection pattern may also occur.
diagnostic_features.quote: BBS lesions are generally confined to the peel and upper pulp, are darker and more angular, and have raised margins. Additionally, when BBS lesions coalesce, they form cracks from which sap oozes out. Note that these necrotic spots are angular and raised, not round and depressed into the pulp like anthracnose lesions.

look_alikes.quote: BBS symptoms may be confused with those caused by the common anthracnose fungus, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, a pathogen that is widespread and ubiquitous in Florida mango groves.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Scientific Name Glomerella cingulata (it also has the name of Colletotrichum gloeosporioides ). Glomerella is the sexual stage of the fungus, and Colletotrichum the asexual stage.

type_of_disease.quote: so fungi that produce dark spots are often given this name

affected_parts.quote: It causes a blight of flowers and young shoots, leaf spots, and fruit rots.

summary.value: Spots start small, black, and irregular on leaves, expanding into large dead areas that dry and fall out. On mature fruit, infections form dark brown to black spots with orange-pink spore masses as the fruit ripens.
summary.quote: At first, the spots are small, black and irregular, often expanding to form large dead areas that dry and fall out. On mature fruits, the fungus remains as pinpoint infections until the fruit ripens; then the infections form dark brown to black spots with orange-pink spore masses

diagnostic_features.value: Glomerella spots on leaves are usually larger than Stigmina spots. On fruit, orange-pink spore masses develop in the centres of dark brown to black spots.
diagnostic_features.quote: Spots of Glomerella are usually larger on the leaves, whereas those of Stigmina are about 6 mm diameter, surrounded by a wide light greenish zone

look_alikes.quote: it is not always easy to distinguish between diseases caused by Glomerella and Stigmina . Spots of Glomerella are usually larger on the leaves, whereas those of Stigmina are about 6 mm diameter, surrounded by a wide light greenish zone (Photos 3-5)

conflicts.note: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides is the asexual (anamorph) stage of Glomerella cingulata; both names are used in literature. The Lucid fact sheet notes: 'it also has the name of Colletotrichum gloeosporioides'. The EDIS BBS source also references Colletotrichum gloeosporioides as the anthracnose pathogen.
